title: 3Sum: sort + two-pointer for remaining pair.
shortTitle: 3Sum: Sort Then Two-Pointer for the Remaining Pair
keyPoints: Sort the array, fix one element, then use opposite-end two pointers on the remaining subarray to find completing pairs.
Duplicate handling at three points: fixed element, left pointer after match, right pointer after match.
O(n squared) time because the O(n log n) sort is dominated by the n times O(n) two-pointer scans.
O(1) extra space beyond the sort and the output list.
The break condition when the fixed element exceeds the target prunes unnecessary iterations.
The same sort-plus-two-pointer template generalises to kSum by recursing with k minus one.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort first, fix one element, then run opposite-end two pointers on the rest, skipping duplicates, to collect all triplets in O(n squared).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **3Sum variant** – find all unique triplets summing to zero using sort plus two-pointer pair search.
- **Fix one, scan two** – the outer loop picks the first triplet member; the inner two-pointer scan finds the completing pair.
- **Duplicate skipping** – three skip points prevent the same triplet from appearing more than once.
- **Time** – O(n squared) total; the O(n log n) sort is absorbed by the quadratic scan.
- **Space** – O(1) extra beyond the sort and the output.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to find every set of three ledger adjustments that net to zero so they cancel out. Rajesh sorts the adjustments, fixes the first one, and uses two fingers from the ends of the rest to find a matching pair that brings the total to zero, skipping repeats so he never reports the same trio twice.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The 3Sum problem asks me to find every unique triplet in an array that sums to zero, and the efficient approach combines sorting with two pointers. I sort the array first, then fix each element as the first member of the triplet. For the remaining part of the array I place a left pointer just after the fixed element and a right pointer at the end, moving them inward based on whether the sum is below, above, or equal to zero.

The detail that separates a correct answer from a buggy one is duplicate handling in three distinct places. I skip a fixed element if it equals the previous fixed element, and after recording a matching triplet I advance the left pointer past repeated values and retreat the right pointer past repeated values before moving both inward. Missing any of these three skips produces the same triplet more than once.

On complexity, sorting is O(n log n), and the fixed-element loop wrapping the linear two-pointer scan is O(n squared), which dominates. Extra space is O(1) beyond the output. That is a big improvement over the naive triple loop which is O(n cubed). The same template generalises to kSum by recursion.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this in the month-end netting service. Ledger adjustments could be positive or negative, and the risk team wanted every unique group of three adjustments that cancelled to zero so they could be closed together. Because duplicate adjustment amounts were common, the three duplicate-skipping points ensured no cancelling trio was ever reported twice.

Remember one sentence: sort the array, fix one element, two-pointer the rest, and skip duplicates at three points for O(n squared) unique triplet detection.
